findings.text: The first sentence tells a newcomer plainly what Athena is and what makes it different, so they can say what the site is about right away.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: The header explains why this page exists: it is a sample of Athena's output. A newcomer understands they are looking at a demonstration, not Athena's own documentation.
findings.source: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files."

findings.text: The next step is linked from the top and listed again at the end, with a repository link, an install command and a sample request. A newcomer knows what to do next.
findings.source: Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself (header) and the "Next steps" section

findings.text: The install step names no prerequisites (a Rust toolchain, model API keys) and does not say what `athena ask` produces or where it runs. A newcomer may get stuck after cloning.
findings.source: Next steps: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" and "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: Only about three sentences cover Athena; everything else is a detailed study of firstmate. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena gets little on how it works or why to choose it, beyond the claim-tracing shown by example.
findings.source: Header lede paragraphs vs. the sections "States of a piece of work" through "Claims and sources"

findings.text: Firstmate's own terms are defined before they are used and again in a glossary. This keeps the study readable for someone who has never seen firstmate.
findings.source: "Start here" with "Words used first" and the "Glossary"

findings.text: Some terms are used but never defined in the glossary, including "endpoint", "heartbeat", "watcher", "brief" and "harness pin". In those places a newcomer has to guess.
findings.source: t8 card: "a secondmate re-reads its pin and needs none, and a secondmate with no endpoint is recovered by the spawn script instead"; t2 claim c9: "after every teardown and heartbeat"

findings.text: This limit is written in Athena's internal terms ("job", "recorded boundary", "edge", "marked read"). A newcomer cannot easily tell that it means nothing was actually run.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f1: "The job gave no recorded boundary for running firstmate, so no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read."

findings.text: The Counters section refers to transition ids before the Transitions section defines them. A first-time reader will see unexplained labels unless they scroll ahead.
findings.source: Counters: "places-held, changed by transitions t1, t3, t4, t9, t11"

findings.text: This points to a folder in Athena's repository without a link. A newcomer won't know where `studies/` is.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from."
